Coinbase launches fixed-rate bitcoin-collateralized loans via Morpho Midnight –
Link
Coinbase added fixed-rate BTC-backed USDC loans through Morpho's "Midnight" product, live on Base since July. The exchange already runs floating-rate Morpho Blue loans with $1.4B+ outstanding against roughly $3B in collateral.
On-chain lending and BTC-collateralized credit keep inching toward the mainstream, and this is another step in that direction.

Avalanche's Helicon mainnet upgrade launches Sept. 22 –
Link
Avalanche is rolling out Helicon today. The upgrade cuts the minimum staking lock-up from 14 days to 48 hours, adds auto-renewing staking, and raises validator uptime requirements.
Better staking capital efficiency could support network activity longer-term, though AVAX's price likely already reflects much of that expectation.

DeFi.text:
​
Just dropped a research note on who is actually buying tokenised assets.
Here’s your TL;DR ↓
– Arrakis looked at 71,697 buyers and $91.3B in gross onchain acquisitions across 10 tokenised dollar-yield products.
– The surprise isn't demand size — it's who's behind it: mostly crypto-native institutions, not traditional TradFi allocators.
– Wallets with $1M+ controlled about 93% of capital while making up only 4% of buyers.
– Of the identifiable $12.4B in demand, about 66% came from DAO and protocol treasuries.
– Most purchases still happen through primary subscription; for most products, DEX entry was only 0%–6%.
– RWA marketing looks less like retail growth and more like institutional B2B sales: awareness, diligence, compliance, then allocation.
– The buyer set is narrow, but the decision process is wide — hidden stakeholders inside funds, exchanges and DAOs still need research, proof and clean risk framing.
– The practical implication: issuers need to market to onchain institutions, especially across EMEA and APAC hours, and build trust before anyone hits subscribe.
Read the full story here:
Marketing RWAs: who is actually buying tokenised assets?

​
Just dropped a research note on who is actually buying tokenised assets.
Here’s your TL;DR ↓
– Arrakis looked at 71,697 buyers and $91.3B in gross onchain acquisitions across 10 tokenised dollar-yield products.
– The surprise isn't demand size — it's who's behind it: mostly crypto-native institutions, not traditional TradFi allocators.
– Wallets with $1M+ controlled about 93% of capital while making up only 4% of buyers.
– Of the identifiable $12.4B in demand, about 66% came from DAO and protocol treasuries.
– Most purchases still happen through primary subscription; for most products, DEX entry was only 0%–6%.
– RWA marketing looks less like retail growth and more like institutional B2B sales: awareness, diligence, compliance, then allocation.
– The buyer set is narrow, but the decision process is wide — hidden stakeholders inside funds, exchanges and DAOs still need research, proof and clean risk framing.
– The practical implication: issuers need to market to onchain institutions, especially across EMEA and APAC hours, and build trust before anyone hits subscribe.
Read the full story here:
Marketing RWAs: who is actually buying tokenised assets?

This is one of the most interesting AI trades I’ve seen yet.

Goldman Sachs has a “Consumer Inertia” basket.

Basically: companies that benefit because customers keep paying, renewing, booking, or buying out of habit.

Today it got crushed.

Planet Fitness: -9.5% $PLNT
LPL Financial: -7.5% $LPLA 
New York Times: -7.2% $NYT 
Schwab: -6.1% $SCHW 
Allstate: -5.5% $ALL 

Why?

Investors are starting to ask what happens when personal AI agents begin shopping around for us.

Imagine an AI that automatically:

- Finds cheaper insurance
- Moves your cash to a better account
- Cancels subscriptions you barely use
- Compares travel prices instantly
- Shops for better financial products

A huge amount of corporate profit depends on friction, complexity, and people simply not bothering to switch.

AI could attack all three.

We’ve spent years asking which jobs AI will replace.

Maybe the bigger question is:

Which business models only work because consumers are too busy to look for a better deal?

Source

tweet.text:
🚨SlowMist TI Alert🚨

Attackers posing as a Web3 company used a remote job interview as a pretext to ask a candidate to deploy and run a project locally:

hxxps://bitbucket[.]org/poc_review58/demoroyalcity

Disguised as a real estate and crypto investment application, RoyalCity contained obfuscated malicious code in tailwind.config.js. Running or building the project can trigger payloads capable of stealing browser credentials and wallet extension data, exfiltrating local files, monitoring clipboard contents, and enabling remote control.

A separate server-side backdoor in errorHandler.js retrieves and executes remote code.

This case closely resembles the recruitment-themed GitHub poisoning attack we previously analyzed, sharing the interview lure, execution through Tailwind, and highly similar payloads for data theft and remote access.

Our previous analysis (https://slowmist.medium.com/threat-intelligence-analysis-of-a-github-poisoning-attack-disguised-as-recruitment-30fe23601305) pr

tweet.text:
This is one of the most interesting AI trades I’ve seen yet.

Goldman Sachs has a “Consumer Inertia” basket.

Basically: companies that benefit because customers keep paying, renewing, booking, or buying out of habit.

Today it got crushed.

Planet Fitness: -9.5% $PLNT
LPL Financial: -7.5% $LPLA 
New York Times: -7.2% $NYT 
Schwab: -6.1% $SCHW 
Allstate: -5.5% $ALL 

Why?

Investors are starting to ask what happens when personal AI agents begin shopping around for us.

Imagine an AI that automatically:

- Finds cheaper insurance
- Moves your cash to a better account
- Cancels subscriptions you barely use
- Compares travel prices instantly
- Shops for better financial products

A huge amount of corporate profit depends on friction, complexity, and people simply not bothering to switch.

AI could attack all three.

We’ve spent years asking which jobs AI will replace.

Maybe the bigger question is:

Which business models only work because consumers are too busy to look for a better deal?

tweet.text:
Announcing The Horowitz Andreessen Academy.

The internet made it possible to know anything. AI makes it possible to do anything.

The best assignments now are problems so hard they cannot be solved without AI. The Academy courses follow the same logic and will be taught by world-class leaders.

The most talented young people today rarely have their sharpest peers within walking distance. Their network is online. Those networks are real, but they're thin.

The next generation will not be taught the way the last one was. The Academy is built for that world, and it begins in San Francisco.

If you're young, hungry and love building things, apply for the Founding Class Fellowship.
